text: Part 3. First, review questions 21 to 25. Come in, Maria. I've read your essay on reducing plastic waste. Let's talk it through. Thanks. I was a bit unsure whether my argument came across clearly. Well, your central claim is that individual action alone isn't enough. That governments and manufacturers have to take the lead that came through very strongly. Good, because that was the point I most wanted to make. You establish it effectively by comparing household choices with decisions made earlier in the production chain. Your example of someone refusing a plastic bag is useful because it shows both the value and the limit of personal choice. The shopper can reduce demand, but cannot redesign packaging or require consistent collection across a whole region. I was careful not to suggest that personal habits are pointless. I meant that they work best when the wider system supports them. That balance is present. Keep the sentence where you say responsibility is shared, because it prevents the argument from sounding absolute. And the writing itself is clear and well organised. What impressed me most though was your use of real examples. The case study of the deposit return scheme in Germany was excellent. I found that really interesting to research. The German case works because you explain what happened rather than merely naming the policy. You show how a payment is added when a container is bought and returned when it comes back. You also compare the return rate before and after the scheme. That is more persuasive than a list of countries. I nearly used three short examples instead. One developed case is stronger here. The clarity of your pros and the overall length are both good, but neither is as distinctive as the concrete evidence. Now there is one weakness. Some of your statistics are quite old. A few of your sources date back to 2009. For a topic that moves this fast, you really need more recent data. I did wonder about that. I found the oldest studies easier to access. I understand but do update them. Also, I'd suggest reorganizing the middle section. At the moment you present all the problems and then all the solutions. It would be stronger to pair each problem with its solution as you go. Now review questions 26 to 30 before the recording continues. That makes sense. It would flow better. Exactly. Start with packaging that is difficult to recycle and follow it immediately with a design response. Then discuss inconsistent collection and the policy that might address it. Your current headings can remain, but each subsection will become a small argument rather than half of a long catalogue. Should I remove the paragraph about public information campaigns? Keep it, but connect it to labeling. Information is useful only if people can identify the correct bin and if the local service accepts the material. That link supports your central position. Exactly. One more thing. Your conclusion is a little short. You introduce an interesting idea about consumer behavior right at the end, but you don't develop it, I'd move that into the main body. I'll do that. What about the length overall? You are within the limit, so expansion is unnecessary. Moving the consumer point will leave space for a final paragraph. That draws the argument together. In that paragraph, state which actors should act first and explain why. Do not introduce another policy at that stage. So the ending should reflect the argument I have already demonstrated. Precisely. A brief qualification would also be useful. National rules vary, so one model may need adapting rather than copying unchanged. The length is fine. Now, in terms of what to do next, first you need to strengthen the evidence so find some newer figures. Second, I'd like you to add a diagram showing how much plastic is recycled. A visual really helps the reader. Then check your referencing because a couple of citations are missing a date. After that, read the whole thing aloud to catch any awkward sentences. And finally, send me the revised draft by email so I can look at it again before you submit. Thank you, that's really helpful. Before you go, set yourself a realistic order. Locate the updated sources first, because they may change a claim elsewhere. Make the structural revisions next, then create the visual once you know which comparison it needs to show. Leave proofreading until those larger changes are complete. I can do the research tomorrow and revise over the weekend. Good. When you read the draft, listen for sentences that run too long as well as obvious errors. Your final message should include both the document and a brief note identifying the sections you changed. Part 3 is complete. Check your answers.
